text:
# Compositing and Blending

Also called: Accumulate, Alternative Compositing Schemes, Blending Modes, First Hit, Front-to-back blending, Maximum Intensity blending, Minimum Intensity blending

## Overview
Compositing and Blending is the final accumulation stage of [direct volume ray casting](#19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md), responsible for integrating the optical properties (color and opacity) of samples along a viewing ray into a single 2D pixel color [S1][S3, unofficial]. It solves the problem of projecting translucent 3D scalar fields onto a 2D image plane by correctly handling depth ordering and light attenuation [S1, S46, unofficial]. What sets this family apart from its siblings is its fundamental reliance on iterative sample accumulation ([compositing](#2436-compositing.md)) and signal reconstruction (interpolation) to approximate the [volume rendering integral](#8682-volume-rendering-integral.md), rather than pre-computing lookup tables (like [Pre-Integration Lookup](2854-pre-integration-lookup.md)) or using discrete binary logic for distributed merging (like [Binary Swap Compositing](3264-binary-swap-compositing.md)) [S1][S2, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All compositing methods in this family operate on a sequence of samples $(c_i, \alpha_i)$ encountered along a ray, where $c_i$ is the sample color (RGB) and $\alpha_i$ is the sample opacity (A) [S1][S2, unofficial]. The core mechanism involves an accumulator state $(C_{acc}, \alpha_{acc})$ initialized to $(0, 0)$ (or background color/opacity) and updated iteratively for each sample [S1][S2, unofficial].

The standard optical model assumes that light is emitted or scattered by the volume and attenuated by absorption [S1]. The [standard front-to-back compositing](#1141-front-to-back-compositing-unpremultiplied.md) equation updates these accumulators for each sample $i$ from front to back:
$$
C_{acc}^{(i)} = C_{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha_{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alpha_i C_i
$$
$$
\alpha_{acc}^{(i)} = \alpha_{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha_{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alpha_i
$$
where $C_{acc}^{(0)} = 0$ and $\alpha_{acc}^{(0)} = 0$ [S12, S43, S50, unofficial]. The term $(1 - \alpha_{acc}^{(i-1)})$ represents the transmittance, i.e., the fraction of light reaching sample $i$ from the camera side [S1, S51, unofficial].

In iterative form using transmittance $T = 1 - \alpha_{acc}$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
C_{final} &\leftarrow C_{final} + c_i \cdot \alpha_i \cdot T \\
T &\leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alpha_i)
\end{aligned}
$$
Where $T$ is initialized to $1.0$ and represents the accumulated transparency $\prod (1-\alpha_j)$ [G].

The final pixel color is often composited over a background color $C_{bg}$ using $C_{final} = C_{acc} + (1 - \alpha_{acc}) C_{bg}$ [S1, S14, unofficial].

Early ray termination is a common optimization where the loop breaks if $\alpha_{acc}$ exceeds a threshold (e.g., 1.0), as further samples contribute negligibly to the color [S10, S12, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Pre-Integration Lookup](2854-pre-integration-lookup.md)
[Pre-Integration Lookup](2854-pre-integration-lookup.md) is a technique that pre-computes the [optical integration](#4646-reconstruction-and-compositing-techniques.md) of light through a volume slab, replacing iterative per-sample compositing with a single texture fetch. It solves the problem of high computational cost and aliasing artifacts associated with low sampling rates in direct volume ray casting by assuming linear data evolution within each slab. It sets itself apart from standard iterative compositing by moving the integration burden to the [CPU](#10688-naive-sdf-generation-cpu.md) or a pre-processing stage, and from sibling methods like [Binary Swap Compositing](3264-binary-swap-compositing.md) by relying on analytical integration of the transfer function rather than [hierarchical data structures](#4133-hierarchical-data-structures.md).

### [Binary Swap Compositing](3264-binary-swap-compositing.md)
[Binary Swap Compositing](3264-binary-swap-compositing.md) is a parallel image merging algorithm used to combine independently rendered sub-images from multiple processors into a final volume-rendered image. It solves the bottleneck problem of naive binary compositing, where processors become idle as the compositing tree narrows, by ensuring every processor participates in every stage of the merge. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Compositing and Blending](2515-compositing-and-blending.md) by explicitly managing distributed memory communication via a binary-swap tree structure, and from [Pre-Integration Lookup](2854-pre-integration-lookup.md) by operating on already-composited sub-images rather than raw samples.

### [Blend Method](3390-blend-method.md)
[Blend Method](3390-blend-method.md) is a [texture-based volume rendering](#4707-texture-based-volume-rendering.md) technique that offloads the compositing operation to graphics hardware by resampling volume slices parallel to the image plane into a frame buffer and using the hardware's blending unit (specifically the "over" operator) to composite them. It differs from the [Planes method](#3027-planes-method.md), which performs compositing in software on the CPU, by leveraging hardware [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) for the accumulation step, making it significantly faster for fully translucent volumes where rays rarely reach full opacity.

### [Screen-space Post-processing](3621-screen-space-post-processing.md)
[Screen-space Post-processing](3621-screen-space-post-processing.md) is a full-screen rendering pass that applies aspect-ratio preserving UV covering, luminance-based bright passes, color grading, underwater RGB channel splitting, [cross-shaped bloom](#4906-bloom.md), 17-tap box blur, and 1-LSB dithering to a scene texture. It differs from [Compositing](2436-compositing.md) by operating on the final rendered image rather than accumulating volume samples along rays.

### [Layered SDF Compositing](3641-layered-sdf-compositing.md)
[Layered SDF Compositing](3641-layered-sdf-compositing.md) is a method for rendering Signed Distance Field ([SDF](#1466-signed-distance-fields-sdf.md)) glyphs by compositing multiple layers (typically a face and one or more outline layers) using [alpha blending](#5750-alpha-blending.md) and pre-multiplied alpha handling. It differs from standard volume [ray casting](#6080-ray-casting.md) by operating on discrete, pre-sampled layers of a 2D texture atlas rather than continuous 3D volume data, allowing for efficient, sharp text rendering with variable-width outlines.

### [Reconstruction and Compositing Techniques](4646-reconstruction-and-compositing-techniques.md)
[Reconstruction and Compositing Techniques](4646-reconstruction-and-compositing-techniques.md) constitute the core mathematical and algorithmic framework for Direct Volume Ray Casting, solving the problem of projecting translucent 3D scalar/vector fields onto a 2D image plane by integrating optical properties along viewing rays. This family is distinguished from sibling methods like [Pre-Integration Lookup](2854-pre-integration-lookup.md) or [Binary Swap Compositing](3264-binary-swap-compositing.md) by its fundamental reliance on iterative sample accumulation (compositing) and signal reconstruction (interpolation) to approximate the volume rendering integral, rather than pre-computing lookup tables or using discrete binary logic for blending.

### [Lighting-Specific Compositing](5940-lighting-specific-compositing.md)
[Lighting-Specific Compositing](5940-lighting-specific-compositing.md) refers to a family of compositing strategies that integrate lighting effects (such as in-scattering, multi-channel illumination, or boundary-aware shading) directly into the ray-casting accumulation loop, rather than treating lighting as a post-process or separate pass. It solves the problem of correctly integrating volumetric light transport and material interfaces within the depth-aware accumulation state. It sets itself apart from standard front-to-back compositing by modifying the sample contribution $g_k$ or opacity $\alpha_i$ based on [lighting models](#2056-lighting-models.md) or geometric cues before blending, and differs from [Final Scene Composition](2722-final-scene-composition.md) by handling lighting within the volume ray-caster rather than compositing final rendered layers.

### [Layer-Centric Volume Rendering Framework](6994-layer-centric-volume-rendering-framework.md)
[Layer-Centric Volume Rendering Framework](6994-layer-centric-volume-rendering-framework.md) is a system architecture that decomposes volume visualization into two distinct phases: rendering small regions of interest (ROIs) as separate [layers, and compositing](#4539-multi-layer-surface-compositing.md) these layers using a rich set of 2D operators. Unlike traditional single-pass ray casting, this method treats the final image as a composition of independent renderings, allowing for intuitive 2D-based user interactions and complex material manipulations. It builds on [Compositing and Blending](2515-compositing-and-blending.md) by extending standard Porter-Duff operators to general functional compositing functions applied to layer textures.

### [MAB Compositing with Gaze-Contingent Blending](8211-mab-compositing-with-gaze-contingent-blending.md)
[MAB Compositing with Gaze-Contingent Blending](8211-mab-compositing-with-gaze-contingent-blending.md) is a gaze-contingent rendering technique that maps framebuffer fragments to a Multi-Anchor Buffer ([MAB](#8219-multiresolution-atlas-buffer-mab.md)) to retrieve and blend color values from different resolution levels based on the distance to the user's gaze. It solves the problem of maintaining high frame rates in immersive VR environments by dynamically adjusting the rendering resolution distribution in real-time, thereby preventing performance fluctuations that cause cybersickness. Unlike standard fixed-resolution compositing, it blends multiple resolution levels simultaneously using smooth-step transitions to ensure unnoticeable visual artifacts between detail levels.

### [Multi-view image blending](9831-multi-view-image-blending.md)
[Multi-view image blending](9831-multi-view-image-blending.md) reduces view-dependent artifacts, such as ghosting and transparency variation, by combining multiple pre-rendered images captured from different camera angles. Unlike single-view texture mapping, which suffers from fading and duplication when the viewpoint changes, this method selects and blends at least three textures to approximate the volumetric appearance. It is distinguished from single-view techniques by its reliance on spatial redundancy across views, at the cost of increased memory bandwidth and selection complexity.

### [Dynamic Job-Scheduling for Grid Volume Rendering](10585-dynamic-job-scheduling-for-grid-volume-rendering.md)
[Dynamic Job-Scheduling for Grid Volume Rendering](10585-dynamic-job-scheduling-for-grid-volume-rendering.md) is a job-scheduling method for distributed volume rendering that dynamically updates sub-volume visibility to determine processing order, overcoming the inefficiency of static sequential scheduling where agents with varying speeds cause bottlenecks.

### [HardSoftRas Blending](10747-hardsoftras-blending.md)
[HardSoftRas Blending](10747-hardsoftras-blending.md) is a blending function that distinguishes between edge pixels (silhouettes/vertical surfaces) and non-edge pixels. It uses weighted averaging for edges and keeps the most frontal color for non-edges, generalizing anti-aliasing and SoftRas.

### Commutative Blend Direct Volume Rendering
A rendering technique for unsorted [cell projection](#26-cell-projection.md) using [optical models](#33-optical-models.md) that lead to a commutative blend function, allowing compositing in arbitrary order [S4]. It applies arbitrary transfer functions via texture lookup, which only affect the generation of the texture map [S4]. Models allowing arbitrary order compositing include maximum intensity projection and restrictions of the full volume density model to either the source term or the absorption term [S4].

### Frame Buffer Copy / Blit
A pass that simply copies the current frame to the output, acting as a simple integration or blit step for the [LAO](#4502-local-ambient-occlusion-lao.md) renderer [S5, unofficial]. It samples the frame buffer using `oColor = texture(uFrame, vPosition)` [S5, unofficial].

### Virtual Dimension Expansion for Compositing
A post-processing step where partial images rendered from blocks of different resolutions are expanded to a common 'virtual dimension' (the highest resolution dimension of the block) before compositing [S6, unofficial]. This allows standard compositing algorithms to work despite varying input resolutions [S6, unofficial]. The virtual dimension can be set to the dimension of the largest subimage in the scene to minimize padding, or fixed to the global high-resolution block size [S6, unofficial].

### Hybrid Compositing (Radix-k)
Hybrid methods like Radix-k combine [direct send](#9377-direct-send-compositing.md) and binary swap approaches depending on the problem setting, adaptively running one or the other based on criteria [S7, unofficial].

### Light Value Blending
Blends four light values (a, b, c, d) into a single packed light value, replacing any zero values with the fourth value before averaging [S8, unofficial]. If a == 0, set a = d; if b == 0, set b = d; if c == 0, set c = d; return `((a + b + c + d) >> 2) & 0xFF00FF` [S8, unofficial].

### Fabric Compositing
A compositing pass that creates an initial fabric-like texture by combining advected noise fields, silhouette data, and lighting [S9, book]. Pixels not part of the geometry are discarded using the depth buffer [S9, book]. The color channels after $k$ iterations are defined as:
$$
R(x,y) = \frac{r \cdot f_{\lambda_2}(x,y)}{8 \cdot f_{\lambda_1}^2(x,y)} + e_{x,y} + \text{light}(\mathcal{L}_{x,y})
$$
$$
G(x,y) = \frac{(1-r) \cdot f_{\lambda_1}(x,y)}{8 \cdot f_{\lambda_2}^2(x,y)} + e_{x,y} + \text{light}(\mathcal{L}_{x,y})
$$
$$
B(x,y) = e_{x,y} + \text{light}(\mathcal{L}_{x,y})
$$
Here $f_{\lambda_1}$ and $f_{\lambda_2}$ are the advected fields $p_{\lambda_1}^k$ and $p_{\lambda_2}^k$. $e_{x,y}$ is the silhouette image. $r$ blends between tensor directions. Squaring the denominator emphasizes differences [S9, book]. The blend factor $r$ is a scalar factor used to blend between the two chosen tensor directions [S9, book]. A separate lighting function `light` manipulates intensity without affecting the base color of the mesh structure, with Blinn-Phong shading providing required depth cues [S9, book].

## Background
Compositing is the final step in [object-order volume rendering](#23-splatting.md), where data is ordered in the correct depth order [S1]. It is often the most expensive step in the object-order approach [S1]. Early implementations included Direct Send, where all processors communicate with each other, assigning image tiles to processors and exchanging data [S1]. Binary Swap was developed to reduce network congestion by dividing communication over $\log_2(N)$ rounds, where $N$ is the number of processors, requiring $N$ to be a power of two [S1]. A modified version, [2-3 Swap](#12223-2-3-swap-compositing.md), was implemented by Yu et al. to overcome the power-of-two limitation [S1]. Peterka et al. proposed Radix-k, a hybrid method combining direct send and binary swap [S1].

The VolumePro system supported Front-to-back blending, Minimum Intensity, and Maximum Intensity blending modes [S2, unofficial]. Other compositing schemes include Accumulate ([standard volume rendering](#1165-standard-volume-rendering-equation.md)), First Hit (rendering an isosurface by taking the first sample that exceeds a threshold), Averaging (producing X-ray-like images), and Maximum Intensity Projection ([MIP](#6635-fast-maximum-intensity-projection-mip.md)) [S3, unofficial]. MIP is often used to extract vessel structures in magnetic resonance angiograms [S3, unofficial].
